Language-Switching Invariance of LLM-as-a-Judge for Hindi Scripts and Hinglish — Step 4 run and results

Data: LLMBar (419 pairwise items) → 387-item human-validated core, rendered in English, Hindi (Devanagari), Romanized Hindi and code-mixed Hinglish. Six judges, two answer orders, temperature 0, Cloudflare AI Gateway (cache off).

Main findings.
  1. All six judges were less accurate in every Hindi-language condition than in English, and each of the 18 judge × language drops is significant after Holm correction (paired McNemar, pHolm ≤ 0.02).
  2. Pooled accuracy: English 78.9%, Devanagari 74.1%, Hinglish 73.3%, Romanized 70.3%. Romanized Hindi is the hardest condition: an item-clustered GEE gives odds ratio 0.60 [0.54, 0.67] for a correct verdict, compared with English.
  3. Judges flip their verdict on 8–25% of identical item/order pairs when only the language/script changes. That is well above their own same-prompt re-run flip rate (0–11%).
  4. Judges are affected differently (variant × judge interaction Wald χ²=26.0, df=15, p=0.038). GPT-OSS-120B is the most robust (−3 pp); Llama-3.3-70B and Claude Haiku 4.5 lose 11–13 pp on Romanized Hindi.
  5. The effect remains when the 12 code-heavy items or the 34 human-fixed items are removed (Table 4).

The 6 unreadable judgments remained unreadable after 3 attempts each: 3 Qwen3 outputs where reasoning was cut off at the token limit, and 3 Llama-3.1-8B refusals. They are kept in the logs and counted as incorrect (a conservative choice). The run made 32,010 API calls, including retries of HTTP 429 rate-limit errors, at an estimated cost of $11.53 (token-based estimate). Every record stores the prompt hash, returned model, translation version, timestamp, token usage and raw response.

2. Method (algorithm)

Algorithm 1: Controlled language-switching meta-evaluation
Input: items D = {(x, y1, y2, g)}, languages L = {en, deva, roman, cm}, judges J, orders O = {AB, BA}
1  for each item d in D, language l in L:  (x, y1, y2)_l ← validated translation T_l(d)   # human-checked
2  for each judge j, item d, language l, order o:
3      prompt ← fixed LLMBar judge template filled with (x_l, first, second) per o
4      r ← j(prompt; temperature=0, no cache);   parse last "Output (a|b)" → pick p ∈ {1,2}
5      if unparseable or API error: retry (≤3 attempts) else store (p, raw, usage, hashes)
6  repeat lines 2–5 for runs k = 1, 2 on a fixed 100-item subset (noise floor)
7  compute accuracy, flip rate, position consistency per (j, l); pair cells on (d, o)
8  test l vs en: exact McNemar per judge (Holm across 18 tests); item-clustered bootstrap CIs (B=2000)
9  pooled model: GEE logistic correct ~ language + judge + order, clustered by item

3. Metrics and equations

For judge \(j\), language \(\ell\), item \(i\), order \(o\): the pick is \(p_{j\ell io}\in\{1,2\}\) and the gold label is \(g_i\).

Accuracy: \[\mathrm{Acc}_{j\ell} = \frac{1}{2|D|}\sum_{i\in D}\sum_{o\in\{AB,BA\}} \mathbb{1}[p_{j\ell io}=g_i]\]

Language-switch flip rate (relative to English): \[\mathrm{Flip}_{j\ell} = \frac{1}{2|D|}\sum_{i,o} \mathbb{1}[p_{j\ell io}\neq p_{j,\mathrm{en},io}]\]

Accuracy gap: \(\Delta_{j\ell}=\mathrm{Acc}_{j\ell}-\mathrm{Acc}_{j,\mathrm{en}}\). Position consistency: \(\mathrm{PC}_{j\ell}=\frac{1}{|D|}\sum_i \mathbb{1}[p_{j\ell i,AB}=p_{j\ell i,BA}]\).

Re-run noise floor: across runs \(k<k'\) on the subset \(D_{100}\), \(\mathrm{SelfFlip}_{j\ell}=\binom{3}{2}^{-1}\sum_{k<k'}\frac{1}{2|D_{100}|}\sum_{i,o}\mathbb{1}[p^{(k)}_{j\ell io}\neq p^{(k')}_{j\ell io}]\), and \(\mathrm{Excess}_{j\ell}=\mathrm{Flip}_{j\ell}-\mathrm{SelfFlip}_{j\ell}\).

Exact McNemar test on the paired cells, with \(b\) = right in English and wrong in \(\ell\), \(c\) = the reverse: \[p = P\big(X\le\min(b,c)\big)\cdot 2,\quad X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(b+c,\tfrac12)\]

GEE logistic model with exchangeable within-item correlation: \[\operatorname{logit} P(y_{ij\ell o}=1)=\beta_0+\beta_\ell+\gamma_j+\delta_o,\qquad \mathrm{OR}_\ell=e^{\beta_\ell}\]

Confidence intervals come from 2000 bootstrap resamples of items (the clusters), so the two orders and the paired cells of an item are resampled together.

Llama-3.3-70B, Claude Haiku and Llama-3.1-8B are almost deterministic (self-flip ≤1%), so almost all of their cross-language flips are caused by the language change. Gemma-4 and Qwen3 have a re-run noise floor of 7–11%. For Gemma on Hinglish, the excess is about 0, so most of its Hinglish flips there are noise.

The full per-judge tables for each subset are in metrics_no_codeheavy.csv and metrics_no_humanfixed.csv. Counting the 6 unreadable judgments as incorrect vs dropping them changes accuracy by at most 0.2 pp (Table 1 shows only the conservative version; both are in the CSV).

6. Limitations (to state in the paper)

  • Translations were made by machine (Gemini 2.5 Pro), checked by Claude Sonnet 4.5, and human-validated by two raters on 251 cells (raw meaning agreement 91%, Gwet's AC1 0.91). A drop in accuracy may partly reflect residual translation quality rather than judge bias, although the effect holds after removing human-fixed items.
  • One benchmark (LLMBar), one prompt template, and six judges accessed through Cloudflare/Anthropic APIs at a fixed date. Results are a measurement for these settings, not a universal claim.
  • Claude Haiku 4.5 belongs to the same family as the verifier model (Claude Sonnet 4.5), not the translator.
  • Cost is a token-based estimate; the exact billing is in the AI Gateway logs.
